summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web tool that helps mission planners and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates, with a focus on the Moon's South Pole. For any site and start date, it uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemerides computed from the lunar surface to track where the Sun and Earth are relative to the local horizon, hour by hour, for 30 days. A horizon engine casts 360 rays over the terrain around the site to detect when mountains block sunlight or the line of sight to Earth. From this it calculates when a lander has solar power, when it can communicate directly with Earth (DTE), how long the longest shadow lasts, and gives a viable/marginal/not-viable verdict against user-defined thresholds. A 3D scene shows the lander, the terrain and Sun/Earth vectors that turn red when blocked, and a comparator puts up to three site/date options side by side. This matters because at the South Pole the Sun stays close to the horizon, so a few days or kilometers can decide whether a mission survives. An Explorer mode with a guided tour and plain language, plus English and Spanish, makes it accessible to anyone.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two critical questions for any lunar landing site and date: will the lander have sunlight to generate power, and will it be able to see Earth to communicate? At the lunar South Pole the Sun moves almost along the horizon and Earth hangs low in the sky, so nearby mountains can cut power or communications for days. The tool makes these conditions visible and comparable, so a team can choose the best site, or react quickly when a launch date slips.

HOW IT WORKS

1. NASA ephemerides: the backend queries the NASA/JPL Horizons API with an observer placed on the lunar surface at the site's latitude, longitude and altitude. It retrieves the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth every hour for 30 days (721 samples), including Earth's libration. Results are cached so the app also works offline.

2. Horizon engine: around each site we model a 36 × 36 km elevation grid (60 m/pixel). From the lander we cast 360 rays, one per degree, and find the highest terrain angle in each direction, correcting for lunar curvature (d²/2R, R = 1737.4 km). The Moon has no atmosphere, so no refraction correction is applied.

3. Mission metrics: each hour, the Sun or Earth is "visible" only if it is above the terrain in that exact direction. From this we derive % of sunlight and DTE availability, countdowns to sunset/earthset, the longest continuous shadow, solar-panel efficiency (vertical Sun-tracking panels near the poles, horizontal elsewhere), all operating windows, and a VIABLE / MARGINAL / NOT VIABLE verdict based on thresholds the user sets.

4. Visualization: a 3D scene of the landing site with lunar curvature and procedural craters, a detailed lander whose antenna points at Earth and whose solar array follows the Sun, and Sun/Earth vectors that turn red and dashed exactly where terrain blocks them. Also included: a full-Moon globe lit by the real Sun direction, a 360° horizon panorama, a sky dome, a timeline animation, and a comparator for up to three site/date scenarios.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Planners can quickly check power and communication windows for candidate South Pole regions such as Shackleton's Connecting Ridge, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton and Haworth, and compare them with historical sites (Apollo 11, Apollo 15) and international missions (Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4).

- Shifting the date and seeing the impact immediately supports contingency planning for launch delays.

- Students and the public can understand why landing at the South Pole is hard, in plain language.

ACCESSIBILITY AND CREATIVITY

Two complete interface modes:

- Explorer, for anyone: yes/no answers, analogies, a glossary, a welcome screen and a 10-step guided tour.

- Engineering: terrain margins, hourly data tables and CSV/JSON export.

The whole interface switches instantly between English and Spanish. Instead of a static table, we turned ephemeris data into an interactive scene where you can literally see a mountain blocking the Sun or Earth.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Python, with FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy and Requests, for the API, the NASA/JPL Horizons client and the horizon engine.

- JavaScript, with Three.js and custom GLSL shaders, for 3D rendering.

- HTML and Tailwind CSS for the interface; Canvas 2D for the charts.

- Self-hosted on a Debian mini PC as a systemd service, published over HTTPS with Tailscale Funnel. All frontend libraries are bundled locally, with no CDN dependency.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy (topocentric ephemerides, curvature, no atmosphere), the conditions specific to the South Pole (low Sun, vertical solar panels), usability for non-experts, bilingual access, offline operation for demos, and honesty about limitations.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The terrain is currently a synthetic demonstration elevation model, not measured topography. The next step is to integrate real LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, NASA LRO) elevation data so horizons and shadows match the real South Pole. We also plan to model the Sun as a disk instead of a point and to increase time resolution.
